newsitem.title: USA: FCC's Hundt wants new laws to spur phone competition.
newsitem.headline: FCC's Hundt wants new laws to spur phone competition.

text.p: The nation's top telephone regulator Thursday said last year's landmark communications law is not working and that Congress needs to amend the act to jump-start competition in the $100 billion local phone market.

Eighteen months after the law's enactment, outgoing Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt said competition has been hampered by lawsuits brought by the Baby Bells and GTE Corp. over FCC implementation of the law.

In a speech that drew mixed responses from lawmakers, Hundt blamed the "legal culture" for the lawsuits and urged Congress to give his agency more power to interpret the act and punish companies that violate FCC rules.

Congress should combine suits against key FCC rules before one court and speed the appeals process, he said. The FCC must now wage fights in U.S. appeals courts nationwide, slowing the entry of long-distance carriers into local calling, he said.

And Hundt called on lawmakers to make it tougher for U.S. courts to throw out FCC rules by ensuring that judges give the agency the benefit of the doubt. He cited a 1984 Supreme Court decision in calling for such "deference."

"By no means am I saying the whole thing needs to be reopened," Hundt said of the law in an interview following a speech to the American Enterprise Institute, a Washington think tank. "Just clear up the weed patch of the legal process."
Key lawmakers declined to fully endorse his proposals. They are expected to hold hearings on the act in coming weeks.

"The problem Reed Hundt is having is that he's trying to implement the act that he would have written instead of the one we wrote," said Rep. W.J. (Billy) Tauzin, the Louisiana Republican who chairs the telecommunications subcommittee.
Sen. John McCain, the Arizona Republican who chairs the commerce committee, said he welcomed Hundt's comments about the law not working. McCain agreed new legislation is needed.
"However, I do not think that giving the FCC more authority to regulate is the answer," he added.
Sen. Herb Kohl, a Wisconsin Democrat, is considering legislation to implement at least some of Hundt's proposals.

Lamakers, long-distance companies such as AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp., and others complain the 1996 law so far has failed to open the local phone monopolies controlled by the regional Bells and GTE.

A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis last month threw out key FCC regulations aimed at doing just that, saying the agency did not have the power to issue rules governing the prices new competitors should pay to hook up to the local phone network.
AT&T called Hundt's speech "timely and provocative," saying it would study his proposals. But a spokesman for GTE said: "He wants the FCC to get special treatment."
-- Combine lawsuits against key FCC rules and decisions into one case that would be heard by one appeals court. The judges would be under deadline to issue rulings.
-- Give the FCC national enforcement powers to impose stiffer penalties on companies that violate FCC rules.
-- Give the FCC legal "deference" for any "reasonable" interpretation of the law.

-- Allow the agency to define on a nationwide basis key terms such as the word "cost" associated with operating a local phone network. That way the definition would not vary from one court to the next.
